title: How Gossip Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore what gossip is and why people do it. They distinguish gossip from rumor (gossip is based on fact and requires a social bond; rumors are hypotheses that explain or express hopes and fears), discuss the common definition of gossip as talk about an absent third party, and note that malicious gossip is only one type of a much more common everyday form. They cover the historical view of gossip as something to stamp out (scold's bridle, Puritans, World War II concerns, workplace attitudes), research methods such as eavesdropping and self-report polls, religious condemnation, Robin Dunbar's grooming-and-language theory, gossip as social control and trust-building (including Toronto cooperation/cheating studies), the idea that gossip began around fire at night, and altruistic gossip warning others about cheaters or slackers. The episode closes with a listener letter about Disney's The Little Mermaid and the Southern Baptist boycott, and sign-off.

entities.name: Grooming, Gossip and the Evolution of Language

segments.title: Opening banter and gossip jokes
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about recording as a two-person show without Jerry and tease each other about gossiping, setting up the topic.

segments.title: What gossip is and isn't
segments.summary: Gossip is defined at its simplest as two or more people talking about an absent third person; it can be positive or negative and is not necessarily harmful.

segments.title: Gossip versus rumor
segments.summary: Following Tracy's article, the hosts list distinctions: gossip is based in fact while rumors are hypotheses; gossip maintains social order while rumors explain the unknown; rumors express hopes or fears. Josh offers his own view that gossip requires a bond between speakers.

segments.title: Malicious versus ordinary gossip
segments.summary: Researchers' extra criteria (private setting, unconfirmed claims, moral judgment in tone) are discussed. The hosts note most gossip is ordinary rather than malicious, and question the statistic that only a small share is malicious.

segments.title: Historical attitudes toward gossip and the scold's bridle
segments.summary: Gossip was long condemned in academia and society; the hosts describe the scold's bridle punishment used in sixteenth and seventeenth century England. Wartime concerns and later workplace efforts to stamp out gossip are described, with the finding that transparent management reduces harmful gossip.

segments.title: How gossip is studied and religious views
segments.summary: Researchers study gossip by eavesdropping in cafeterias, and self-report polls estimate gossip time. Major world religions, including Christianity via Leviticus, Judaism, and Buddhism, view gossip negatively.

segments.title: Robin Dunbar's grooming and language theory
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Robin Dunbar's book Grooming, Gossip and the Evolution of Language, which argues language evolved as vocal grooming, letting primates maintain alliances more efficiently. Discussion covers how gossip serves similar bonding purposes, plus entertainment, information exchange, and moral lessons.

segments.title: Break and sidetrack
segments.summary: Brief break and off-topic discussion of Death Wish and Charles Bronson films before returning to the topic.

segments.title: Gossip as social control and trust
segments.summary: Gossip is described as a way to keep tabs on others in growing groups, to build trust, and to enforce social control. Dr. Fineberg's University of Toronto studies showed non-cooperators behaved better when they knew they might be gossiped about. The Puritans are described as societies run on gossip.

segments.title: Origins of gossip: foraging, campfires, and cheater warnings
segments.summary: Hypotheses are offered that gossip arose from foraging and needing to know group members' abilities, and around the first campfire. Studies of Kalahari Bushmen are mentioned. Experiments show people warn others about cheaters, and altruistic gossip is illustrated with a choir example. Gossip is described as blowing off steam without directly solving problems.

segments.title: Listener mail: The Little Mermaid
segments.summary: Lindsay writes about growing up with a Southern Baptist household that boycotted Disney, watching the Golden Films version of The Little Mermaid, and later seeing the Hans Christian Andersen original. The hosts respond to her thanks for sidetracking.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give contact information for social media, email, and the website and sign off.
